newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-TI says on target for further growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-TI says on target for further growth.

text.p: International engineering firm TI Group Plc unveiled a solid advance in profits on Wednesday and predicted further growth this year, despite difficult conditions in some European markets.
Pretax profits for 1996 were up 26 percent at 232.2 million pounds ($369 million) last year, with underlying profits before an exceptional gain from disposals up 16 percent at 211.1 million pounds.
Sales rose to 1,757 million pounds from 1,703 million in 1995, with underlying sales growth up eight percent after adjusting for acquisitions and disposals.

Chairman Sir Christopher Lewinton said the group was well positioned by region and product to make further progress in 1997 despite what he said would be "another challenging year, particularly in Europe."

In particular the company said its Bundy division making specialist tubing had faced the brunt of the problems, which were in European automotive markets. But weakness in France and Sweden had been offset by increased output in Britain, Spain and Germany.

Overall the group expected to continue expanding through organic growth and further bolt-on acquisitions, having widened its geographical spread last year thanks to accelerating growth in Asia Pacific and Latin America.

Investors endorsed the confident note, sending TI's share price up 17-1/2 pence to 581-1/2 by 1030 GMT. "The results looked solid and the dividend seems to have impressed people," one share trader said.
The final dividend was increased a penny to 9.75 pence, making 14.5p for the year, up from 13.1p in 1995.
Earnings were up 29 percent at 34.1p, and up 16 percent at 30 pence before the exceptional gains of 21.1 million pounds.
Analysts had forecast pre-tax profits of between 208 and 215 million pounds and a dividend of 14.3 pence.

The firm said it spent another 275 million pounds on more bolt-on acquisitions last year to add to its core businesses of John Crane mechanical seals and engineering polymers, Bundy tubing, mainly for the automotive and refrigeration markets, and Dowty Aerospace.
"We have had another very good year," said Lewinton.
"Our order books are healthy and our current trading is in line with expectations so all in all we are very pleased," he told Reuters in a post-results interview.

"All our core businesses have grown in double-digit terms for many many years now and they are still not bumping their heads against the ceiling...TI in my view can keep doing this for many many years."
Lewinton said TI would continue its policy of the last five years of steadily making bolt-on acquisitions.
"There are plenty of opportunities for bolt-ons," he said. "We have very good (interest) cover, we have low gearing and we have strong cash generation."

After acquisitions TI had net debt of 68 million pounds at the end of 1996, to put gearing at 21 percent of net assets of 325 million pounds. Operating activities generated gross cash of 229.7 million pounds from 224.7 million pounds in 1995 and interest cover rose to 43 times operating profits from 22 times in 1995.

But organic growth would also play a part. "It (organic growth) is central to TI's success," Lewinton said. "From new products, new applications of existing products, from new markets, expeanding the customer base, by cost reductions and by aggressive pricing policies."

Sales in North America rose to 750.8 million pounds from 680.3 million in 1995. Mainland European sales dipped to 536.2 million from 555 million pounds but sales in markets outside north America and Europe rose to 248.4 million pounds from 211.7 million in 1995.
British markets accounted for sales of 221.2 million pounds, down from 256.3 million a year ago. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
